learningObjective: Recognize scenarios where loop unrolling degrades rather than improves performance.

canonicalClaims.claim: Aggressive loop unrolling can degrade performance by increasing code size beyond the instruction cache's capacity and, on GPUs, by inflating per-thread register usage past the spill threshold.
conditions: The unrolled body's total instruction count exceeds the I-cache working set (CPU) or per-thread register budget (GPU).
The un-unrolled loop's overhead was already amortized over enough work per iteration.
nonImplications: Does not imply unrolling is generally harmful; small unroll factors often help exposed ILP and reduce branch overhead.
Does not imply compilers cannot self-tune; production compilers use heuristics.

misconceptions.claim: Full unrolling of a fixed small trip-count loop violates SSA form.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Full unrolling replaces the loop with straight-line code — this is the canonical way to eliminate a loop and is SSA-preserving.

misconceptions.claim: Unrolling never helps with data-dependent memory accesses.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Unrolling can expose ILP between independent lanes, allowing the CPU to issue multiple independent loads even when each address is data-dependent.

misconceptions.claim: Unrolling is a free optimization because it only affects the front-end (branch/increment); the back-end always benefits.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Back-end register allocation and I-cache pressure both scale with unrolled body size; unrolling is not free.

misconceptions.claim: GPU compilers always ignore unroll pragmas because loops on GPUs execute in warp-lockstep.
misconceptions.whyWrong: nvcc / Triton respect unroll pragmas; warp lockstep is orthogonal to per-thread control flow unrolling.

performanceScenarios: Unrolling an 8-element inner GEMM K-loop is beneficial (exposes ILP); unrolling the outer M-loop by 8× rarely helps and inflates code.
